sub_unit_name: Plastics: Definition and characteristics- thermoplastic and thermosetting plastics

content.title: What are Plastics?
content.description: Plastics are high molecular weight synthetic or semi-synthetic polymeric materials that can be moulded into desired shapes by the application of heat and pressure.

content.content: Plastics are among the most widely used engineering materials because they are lightweight, durable, corrosion-resistant, inexpensive, and easy to manufacture. Depending on their behavior on heating, plastics are broadly classified into thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics.

content.title: Engineering Importance
content.content: Plastics have replaced metals in many applications due to their low weight, good strength, chemical resistance, and ease of fabrication.

Plastics are polymeric materials that become soft when heated and can be moulded into different shapes. After cooling, they retain the desired shape and are widely used in household, industrial, medical, and electrical applications.

items.question: Light Weight
items.answer: Plastics have low density, making them easy to transport and handle.

items.question: Chemical Resistance
items.answer: They resist corrosion, acids, alkalis, and many chemicals.

items.question: Electrical Insulation
items.answer: Most plastics are excellent electrical and thermal insulators.

items.question: Easy Processing
items.answer: They can be easily moulded, extruded, or fabricated into different shapes.

items.question: Durability
items.answer: Plastics have good toughness, long service life, and require less maintenance.

content.content: Thermoplastics soften on heating and harden on cooling. This process can be repeated several times without significant chemical change, making them recyclable and easy to reshape.

content.title: Examples of Thermoplastics
content.content: Polyethylene (PE), Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC), Polystyrene (PS), Polypropylene (PP), Nylon and Acrylic.
Thermosetting plastics undergo permanent hardening during heating due to cross-linking of polymer chains. Once set, they cannot be softened or reshaped by reheating.

content.title: Examples of Thermosetting Plastics
content.content: Bakelite, Melamine, Urea-formaldehyde resin, Epoxy resin and Phenol-formaldehyde resin.
Comparison of Thermoplastics and Thermosetting Plastics

items.question: Thermoplastics
items.answer: Used for pipes, bottles, packaging materials, toys, automobile parts, and electrical insulation.

items.question: Thermosetting Plastics
items.answer: Used for electrical switches, plug boards, handles, adhesives, laminates, and circuit boards.

items.question: Medical Uses
items.answer: Used in disposable syringes, IV bags, medical containers, and prosthetic devices.

items.question: Industrial Uses
items.answer: Used in machine components, insulation materials, storage tanks, and protective coatings.

content.title: Exam Tip
content.content: The most frequently asked question is the comparison between thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics along with suitable examples.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: They are lightweight, durable, and corrosion resistant.
Thermosetting plastics harden permanently after heating.
PVC, PE, and Nylon are thermoplastics.
Bakelite, Melamine, and Epoxy are thermosetting plastics.
